name: Chrau
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Thomas, David D. 1971. Chrau Grammar (Oceanic Linguistics Special Publications 7). Univ. of Hawaii Press — on archive.org only as lending-restricted scan; Rosetta phoneme extract read but contains no stress statement

new_statements.quote: Chrau words may be of one or two syllables. In 2-syllable words the second syllable is always accented and pronounced very distinctly. The first syllable is almost never accented, and its vowel is often variable or obscure; so we have usually written the vowel of the first syllable as a, though in some situations, especially next to a s, y, j, or d we have written the vowel as i, or occasionally as u or o. [...] Chrau does not have tones like Vietnamese nor registers like Cambodian.
new_statements.citation: Thomas, David & Thổ Sàng Lục. 1966. Ngữ-vựng Chrau / Chrau Vocabulary: Chrau–Việt–English (Tủ sách ngôn-ngữ dân-tộc thiểu-số Việt-Nam, cuốn 1). Saigon: Bộ Giáo-dục [Summer Institute of Linguistics].

In 2-syllable words the second syllable is always accented and pronounced very distinctly. The first syllable is almost never accented, and its…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The Chrau phonological word is at most disyllabic (presyllable + main syllable); stress/accent falls on the final (main) syllable, the presyllable being unstressed with a reduced, non-contrastive vowel; monosyllables are trivially stressed. Corroborated by Dorothy Thomas 1966 (MKS 2) p.8 §4 'If a two-syllable word is emphasized, only the main (final) syllable is on the higher pitch' and p.11 §5.1 'The pre-syllable of a two syllable word... is inherently de-stressed'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned (words are maximally two syllables; presyllable described as inherently de-stressed).
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost never accented' for the first syllable (no specific exceptions listed); Dorothy Thomas 1966 notes an emphasized negative proclitic n- presyllable can carry emphatic high pitch (n'huch), an intonational, not lexical, effect. Loans from Vietnamese lose lexical tone when assimilated.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a dictionary introduction (orthography/grammar notes), Xuân Lộc dialect; Dorothy Thomas 1966 treats stress within sentence intonation (emphasis raises pitch on the main syllable only). Language explicitly described as non-tonal, non-register.
new_statements.identity_note: Both first-hand sources describe the Xuân Lộc-area dialect of Chrau (Thomas & Lục 1966 intro: 'We have followed in general the dialect spoken around Xuân Lộc'; Dorothy Thomas 1966 fn.1: 'The dialect studied here is that of the Xuan Lôc area... Other dialects have different intonation patterns'). Language-level glottocode chra1242; no separate dialect glottocode needed.

sources.note: p. xv: words are one or two syllables; in two-syllable words the second syllable is always accented and pronounced very distinctly; the first syllable is almost never accented and its vowel is variable/obscure. Also: Chrau has no tones or registers; emphatics/negatives carry high intonational pitch.

sources.citation: Thomas, David. 1992. On sesquisyllabic structure. Mon-Khmer Studies 21: 206-210.
sources.note: General claim: sesquisyllabic structure results from stress shift to the final syllable of the word; Chrau cited (Thomas 1971:30-44) as type (ii) with CC- vs CəC- presyllable contrast (play 'fruit' vs palay). No Chrau-specific stress sentence.

sources.citation: Thomas, Dorothy M. 1966. Chrau intonation. Mon-Khmer Studies 2: 1-13.
sources.note: p.8 §4: an emphasized word is stressed; 'If a two-syllable word is emphasized, only the main (final) syllable is on the higher pitch.' p.11 §5.1: 'The pre-syllable of a two syllable word is very frequently on low pitch. As this syllable is inherently de-stressed, there is no change in the amount of stress.' Chrau is non-tonal with sentence intonation (p.1).
